facts.claim: The joint that looks like a backward-bending knee on a flamingo's leg is actually its ankle; the real knee sits higher up, hidden under the feathers.
In a 2017 Biology Letters study, a dead flamingo held upright settled into a stable one-legged pose with no muscle activity at all.
The same flamingo bodies could not be held stable in a two-legged pose.
The researchers also stood eight live juvenile Chilean flamingos at Zoo Atlanta on a force plate to measure how much they swayed.
The live flamingos swayed less when they dozed off on one leg than when they were awake.
The study concluded that standing on one leg takes flamingos very little muscular effort, because the pose is held passively by the body's mechanics.
A 2010 Zoo Biology study of captive Caribbean flamingos found that more birds rested on one leg when standing in water than on land.
In that study, resting on one leg became less common as the temperature rose, which suggests the pose helps flamingos keep body heat.
